overview: Seeka Limited is one of New Zealand's two largest kiwifruit post-harvest operators, providing an integrated supply chain service from orchard to market across New Zealand and Australia. The company operates 12 packhouse and coolstore facilities covering all major NZ growing regions, owns and leases orchards, and provides retail and wholesale services through its SeekaFresh division. Seeka supplies predominantly to Zespri, the global single-desk kiwifruit marketer, packed a record 47.1 million class 1 trays in 2025, and has delivered consecutive record profits in FY2024 and FY2025 following a period of weather-related losses in 2022-2023.

business_model.summary: Highly seasonal fee-for-service and integrated produce business with approximately 70-90% of gross profit generated in the first half of the calendar year coinciding with the NZ kiwifruit harvest (March-June). Post-harvest operations earn per-tray packing and coolstorage fees from independent growers. Orcharding generates cost-plus margins or profit shares from short and long-term leased orchards that Seeka manages and harvests. SeekaFresh earns commissions on retail sales, wholesale margins, and value-added product revenues. Australian operations are an integrated grower-handler-retailer. The business has strong operating leverage: FY2024 saw a 44% volume increase drive a 193% EBITDA improvement; conversely, FY2023 low volumes caused a $21m pre-tax loss.
business_model.customer_type: B2B: primarily Zespri (kiwifruit export marketer) and independent NZ growers for post-harvest/orcharding. B2B/B2C: SeekaFresh serves large-format NZ retailers, Asian exporters, and runs a wholesale fresh produce market.
business_model.geographic_mix: New Zealand approximately 95% of revenue, Australia approximately 5%. NZ operations span Northland (Kerikeri, Orangewood), Coromandel (Peninsula), Bay of Plenty (Katikati, Aongatete, Work Road, Huka Pak, Oakside, KKP, Transpack, OPAC), and Gisborne. Bay of Plenty provides approximately 85% of Seeka's kiwifruit supply.
business_model.seasonality: Highly seasonal - approximately 70-90% of annual gross profit earned in H1 (January-June). This creates significant working capital requirements during harvest and large period-to-period earnings swings within the year.

main_competitors: EastPack Limited (Te Puke-based co-operative, NZX-listed, largest operator ~30% market share)
competitive_position.market_position: Seeka is one of the two largest kiwifruit post-harvest operators in New Zealand alongside EastPack. Seeka packed 47.1 million class 1 trays in 2025 and 43.0 million in 2024 from a total NZ industry of approximately 200-215 million trays, representing roughly 20-25% market share. Seeka is also the largest single kiwifruit grower (by owned/leased hectares managed) in both New Zealand and Australia. It is the only listed pure-play kiwifruit company on the NZX.

moat_factors.factor: Scale and geographic diversification of infrastructure
moat_factors.description: 12 packhouse facilities across all major NZ growing regions (Northland, Coromandel, Bay of Plenty, Gisborne) plus Australian assets. Capacity exceeding 50 million trays. Scale enables investment in automation (Reemoon technology), data visualisation, and grower management tools unattainable by smaller operators. Regional spread reduces single-event weather risk.

Seeka's orcharding operations grew approximately 40% of the fruit it handled in post-harvest in FY2024, rising to over 40% in 2025. This vertical integration creates a captive volume base that reduces revenue volatility versus post-harvest-only operators and deepens grower relationships. Long-term lease co-investments with iwi (Raukokore) and government agency Kanoa further entrench supply commitments.

Multi-year orchard management contracts, a grower loyalty share scheme, and integrated services create switching costs and loyalty. High pre-season grower sign-up rates (highlighted by management as a key metric). Seeka app provides real-time fruit tracking from NZ packhouse to offshore markets, adding grower value.

KKP automated packing machine (in 2nd full season in 2024), Oakside and Gisborne upgrades, and 2026 Reemoon installations at Kerikeri and Huka Pak have structurally reduced per-tray costs. Total expenses per tray were down 19% in FY2024 despite 44% volume growth. Automation creates a competitive advantage in labour cost and throughput management.

Seeka is an accredited Zespri Registered Supplier with BioGro-certified organic packhouses. These accreditations are necessary to participate in the single-desk export programme and signal quality standards to growers. Seeka's track record of low onshore fruit loss and excellent offshore quality is a competitive differentiator for grower retention.

weaknesses: Revenue is fundamentally volume-driven and highly sensitive to weather, creating binary year-to-year earnings outcomes with no natural hedge
High fixed-cost base (12 packhouses, coolstores, 650+ permanent staff) amplifies earnings volatility when volumes decline
EastPack and other co-operatives can offer growers equity ownership stakes that Seeka, as a public company, cannot match
Concentrated customer: Zespri as single-desk exporter limits pricing leverage on post-harvest service fees
SeekaFresh and Australian businesses remain subscale contributors relative to total capital employed

growth_drivers: NZ kiwifruit industry volume growth: Zespri's five-year plan targets 236 million trays by 2030 (from 214 million in 2025, +10%). The 2025/26 NZ season is forecast at a record ~215 million trays with up to 400 ha of new SunGold licences releasing in 2026. Seeka's packhouse capacity (>50m trays) is in place to capture its share of industry growth without major additional capital.

SunGold (Gold3) variety shift: SunGold is the premium higher-margin variety with growing per-hectare yields. Seeka packed 29.9 million SunGold trays in H1-2025 (63% of total), up 10% on prior year. Seeka's SunGold yields averaged 14,436 trays/ha in 2025, up 7%. Continued SunGold expansion underpins earnings quality improvement.

Post-harvest automation delivering structural cost reduction: Reemoon technology installations at Kerikeri and Huka Pak for the 2026 season, plus evaluation of a 'lights-out' fully automated coolstore, will allow more fruit to be handled at lower per-unit costs. FY2024 already demonstrated 19% cost-per-tray reduction. These investments defend margins as volumes grow.

Orchard development pipeline entering production: 70+ hectares co-developed with iwi in Raukokore (first crop 2025, volumes growing), plus $7.1m invested in 15 ha kiwifruit and 13 ha avocado on long-term leased land. These orchards will progressively increase Seeka's captive volume supply through 2026-2030.

Australian business scale-up from new developments: $17.2m invested in new Australian orchard developments (64 ha kiwifruit, new pear varieties, jujube expansion). FY2024 Australian kiwifruit production up 166% following a new Psa crop protection programme. New orchards scheduled to start producing in 2026 will lift Australian EBITDA materially from the current $6-7m H1 run rate.

Debt reduction reducing financial drag: Net bank debt fell from $172m (2023) to $137m (2024) to $100m (December 2025). Lower interest costs (down from ~$17m in FY2024) are flowing through to after-tax returns. Further debt reduction improves dividend capacity and provides headroom for strategic optionality.

Supplementary packing categories improving asset utilisation: Citrus (14m kg contracted packing in 2024) and persimmon (1.5m kg) use packhouse capacity during off-peak kiwifruit periods. Banana ripening and tropical fruit import and conditioning via SeekaFresh add year-round revenue to the fixed-cost base.

Value-added products and diversification: SeekaFresh avocado oil (Olivado acquisition 2025), Kiwi Crush dietary supplement, avocado oil, and wholesale fresh produce market provide modest but growing diversified revenue streams.

business.description: Kiwifruit yields are highly sensitive to growing conditions. Seeka's EBITDA ranged from $26m (FY2023, low volumes from Cyclone Gabrielle and drought) to $96m (FY2025, record volumes) in just three years. The Bay of Plenty provides approximately 85% of Seeka's kiwifruit supply, creating geographic concentration risk. Inadequate winter chill, spring frost, wind damage, water stress, and cyclones can each materially reduce volumes.

Approximately 60% of Seeka's revenue is generated through the Zespri system. Zespri holds the mandated single-desk export licence under NZ Kiwifruit Export Regulations. Any regulatory change removing or weakening this mandate, changes to Zespri's pool allocation methodology, or shifts in Zespri's service fee expectations would directly impact Seeka. Seeka has limited negotiating leverage with Zespri given its scale advantage.

business.risk: Grower retention and competition for supply
business.description: EastPack and other co-operative operators can offer growers equity ownership that Seeka cannot as a public company. Pre-season grower signup rates are a critical operational metric. Loss of significant grower supply to competitors reduces volumes and increases per-unit fixed costs disproportionately.

Psa-V bacterial canker has been endemic in NZ kiwifruit since 2010 and remains a persistent yield and vine health risk. The SunGold Gold3 variety has better Psa tolerance but is not immune. A new virulent Psa strain or adverse weather creating conditions favourable to Psa proliferation could impact vine productivity across Seeka's growing and post-harvest network. Australian operations are also Psa-affected, with a new crop protection programme implemented from 2024.

The high fixed-cost structure (packhouses, coolstores, permanent workforce) means a reduction in volumes creates a disproportionate EBITDA decline. A return to FY2023-level volumes (~30m trays) from FY2025's record 47m would likely produce a pre-tax loss. This binary earnings profile is the fundamental investment risk in the stock.

financial.description: Net bank debt of $100.3m at December 2025 (down significantly from $172m peak). Banking covenants include a 3.25x net leverage ratio and 2.00x interest cover ratio. Seeka required covenant waivers in mid-2023 following the Cyclone Gabrielle crop losses. A return to poor growing conditions could challenge covenant compliance again, particularly if debt reduction slows. Banking facility is a sustainability-linked loan of $201m total.

The seasonal business requires significant working capital to fund harvest operations, packhouse costs, and grower advance programmes in H1 before cash is collected from Zespri later in the season. Peak working capital needs require substantial drawdown of the banking facility in the first half. At June 2025, trade and other receivables were $121.8m with $40.9m in advances to growers outstanding.

The 2024 NZ legislation removing tax deductibility of building depreciation created a $12.5m one-off non-cash deferred tax charge and increased total deferred tax liabilities to $41.7m (FY2024). This creates an ongoing wedge between NPBT and reported NPAT, reducing stated EPS relative to economic earnings.

Australian operations (~5% of revenue) are conducted in AUD creating translation risk. Some USD exposure exists through Zespri's export pricing. Currency movements are secondary in magnitude to volume and operating risks.

regulatory.description: Seeka employs over 1,200 RSE (Recognised Seasonal Employee) workers from Pacific nations plus approximately 1,200 other seasonal staff. RSE scheme quotas, immigration policy, and Accredited Employer Work Visa conditions directly affect labour availability and cost during the critical harvest window. Labour supply constraints eased in 2024 (first time in five years all shifts fully staffed) but remain policy-dependent and could re-tighten.

Zespri's export monopoly is granted under NZ Kiwifruit Export Regulations and periodically comes under review. Any change to the regulatory framework would restructure the kiwifruit supply chain and could fundamentally alter grower-packhouse commercial relationships.

Seeka is subject to XRB's NZ Climate Standards NZ CS 1-3. Seeka's absolute emissions rose 48% in FY2024 to 26,682 tonnes CO2e due to higher volumes. Increasing emissions intensity during high-volume years creates potential compliance and reputational risks as emissions reporting and carbon pricing frameworks develop.

International market access for NZ kiwifruit depends on phytosanitary standards managed by MPI and Zespri. Any new biosecurity detections, pest incursions, or quality failures could trigger market access restrictions affecting the entire industry supply chain.

macro.risk: Climate change and extreme weather events
macro.description: The 2023 season was severely impacted by Cyclone Gabrielle, which caused significant yield losses in Hawke's Bay, Gisborne, and parts of the Bay of Plenty. Climate research indicates that the core Bay of Plenty growing region may face increasing production challenges from changing weather patterns including reduced winter chill, increased drought frequency, and more intense cyclonic events. Seeka is responding with regional diversification and rootstock research but cannot fully mitigate systemic weather risk.

Zespri achieved record global sales of NZ$5.14b in 2024/25 with 220.9m trays and strong per-tray returns. However, Zespri's global licensing programme has expanded SunGold production in Italy, France and other Northern Hemisphere markets, which will eventually create more supply competition for the NZ-grown premium. Unauthorized Chinese SunGold production (7,850+ hectares) also dilutes variety positioning, though Zespri has been winning legal battles against it.

Management has flagged electricity and packaging as major ongoing cost pressures. NZ labour costs (minimum wage, RSE scheme rates) continue to rise. These input cost pressures can reduce margin per tray and limit the benefit of volume growth. Automation is Seeka's primary mitigation.

execution.description: Seeka has $17.2m committed to new Australian orchard developments entering production from 2026. The Australian business has historically been loss-making or marginally profitable (EBITDA $0.7m FY2023, improving to $6.4m H1-2025). Achieving scale and acceptable returns on invested capital requires successful Psa management, crop quality improvement, and market development in a geography where Seeka lacks its NZ scale advantages.

The Reemoon technology installations at Kerikeri and Huka Pak for 2026 represent significant capital commitments. Integration complexity, commissioning downtime during harvest, and the need to optimise technology for each fruit type and quality profile creates execution risk. The KKP automated line took multiple seasons to reach its performance targets.

New Chair Mark Dewdney (appointed December 2024) and director Hayley Gourley (January 2025) replaced long-serving Ashley Waugh (10 years) and Fred Hutchings (12 years as Chair). Board transition during a period of strategic momentum is manageable given CEO Michael Franks' operational continuity, but the full value of new board relationships and oversight style is still being established.

macro_factors.industry_outlook: The NZ kiwifruit industry is in a sustained growth phase with strong structural foundations. Zespri recorded NZ$5.14 billion in global sales in 2024/25 (220.9 million trays), delivering NZ industry direct returns exceeding $3 billion for the first time. Zespri's five-year plan targets 236 million trays by 2030 (up 10%), with SunGold projected to grow 17% to 163.5m trays and RubyRed more than doubling. The 2025/26 NZ season is forecast to produce approximately 215-220 million trays at a record level. The NZ kiwifruit orchard area has expanded to approximately 15,400 hectares across 2,800+ growers at a CAGR of 1.4% since 2013, with up to 400 hectares of new SunGold licences being released annually through 2029. The key uncertainty is the competitive impact of Northern Hemisphere licensed SunGold production (Italy, France) on per-tray returns over the 5-10 year horizon.
macro_factors.cyclicality: High operational cyclicality within years (H1-heavy with 70-90% of annual gross profit) and significant year-to-year swings driven by harvest volumes. Seeka's EBITDA ranged from $26m (FY2023) to $96m (FY2025) within three years, demonstrating the binary nature of the business. Unlike typical agriculture, however, the industry benefits from Zespri's single-desk coordination which provides some demand-side stability through premium market management.
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: Moderate. Net bank debt of $100m at December 2025 on a variable-rate sustainability-linked facility means falling NZ OCR rates (which the RBNZ cut aggressively through 2024-2025) directly reduce interest expenses. FY2024 interest expense was $12.3m; this should decline toward $7-9m in FY2025 and beyond as debt reduces and rates fall. Further debt reduction through FY2026 will progressively reduce this sensitivity.
key_input_costs: Labour: largest cost driver - approximately 650 permanent staff plus 1,200 RSE seasonal workers and 1,200 other seasonal staff. Direct employee expenses were $81.4m in FY2024.

Electricity: powers packhouses and coolstores, a major operating expense subject to NZ electricity market pricing. Seeka is installing solar (220kW added at Kerikeri in 2024) and transitioning to natural refrigerants.
Packaging materials: trays, cartons, labels scale directly with volumes. Inflationary pressures noted by management as an ongoing cost challenge.
Refrigerants: transitioning to natural refrigerants to reduce both operational costs and emissions. Refrigerant leaks are the largest Category 1 emissions source.
Fuel: transport fleet for orchard-to-packhouse logistics and outbound distribution.

recent_developments.event: FY2025 full year results (year ended December 2025): Revenue ~$440m (+7% on FY2024's $411m), EBITDA ~$96m (+26%), NPBT ~$48m (+62%), NPAT $32m, EPS $0.76 (vs normalised $0.51 in FY2024). Net bank debt down 27% to $100.3m from $137.3m. Declared $0.25/share dividend payable 15 April 2026 (fully imputed, DRP applies). Company entered 2026 'in great shape' per CEO but provided no specific volume guidance for 2026 season.

H1-2025 interim results: Revenue $307.9m (+8%), EBITDA $83.5m (+22%), NPBT $59.4m (+32%), NPAT $37.8m (+121%). Packed 47.1m class 1 trays (+10% vs H1-2024's 43.0m). Net bank debt $130.6m (down $40.2m YoY). Full year NPBT guidance raised to $35-39m (from $33-37m). Declared $0.15/share dividend for October 2025.

Seeka purchased assets of Olivado, resetting SeekaFresh's avocado oil manufacturing and marketing business. Provides local capacity to process oil-grade avocado in Northland. Transaction was described as minor but adds integrated processing capability to the SeekaFresh segment.
Seeka banked $64.8m in July 2025 from seasonal grower advance repayments and post-harvest cash collections, significantly reducing net bank debt in the period immediately after the H1 balance date.

Ruby Roo (new red nashi variety developed by Plant and Food Research/Prevar) launched into Australian market, grown on Seeka's Australian orchards. Diversifies Australian product portfolio beyond kiwifruit and traditional nashi.

Mark Dewdney became Chair of the Board, replacing Fred Hutchings who retired after 12 years. Hayley Gourley (appointed January 2025) brings new independent perspective. Board now has three new directors appointed over the past 12 months as part of planned board renewal.

FY2024 results (year ended December 2024): Revenue $411m (+37%), EBITDA $76m (+193%), NPBT $29.7m (vs $21m loss in 2023). Record profit before tax driven by 44% volume uplift to 43.0m class 1 trays. Dividends reinstated after two years: $0.10/share paid January 2025 and $0.05/share paid April 2025. Net debt reduced $35.1m to $137.3m.

Zespri published updated Five-Year Outlook targeting 236 million trays by 2030 from 214 million in 2025 (10% growth). SunGold projected to grow 17% to 163.5m trays; RubyRed to more than double. Up to 400 hectares of new SunGold licences to be released in 2026 (up from 350ha previously signalled). These industry volume targets underpin Seeka's long-term packhouse utilisation outlook.

Seeka's orcharding business co-invested with iwi and Kanoa (government economic development agency) to develop approximately 70 hectares of new kiwifruit orchards in the Raukokore region. Initial orchards produced their first crop in 2025 with volumes forecast to grow as orchards enter full production.

items.notes: Driven by record 47.1m class 1 NZ kiwifruit trays, strong SeekaFresh and Australian segment performance. H1-2025 alone was $307.9m.
H1-2025 EBITDA was $83.5m, confirming the heavily H1-weighted earnings profile. Full year EBITDA of $96m implies H2 EBITDA of approximately $12.5m.

items.vs_prior: actuals (+62% on FY2024 $29.7m; record). Beat top of guidance range by $9m.
items.notes: Benefited from lower interest costs and additional efficiency gains in H2. H1 NPBT alone was $59.4m but includes H2 interest and overheads that reduce full year figure.
NPAT $32m on approximately 42 million shares. FY2024 EPS of $0.21 was depressed by $12.5m one-off deferred tax charge; normalised was $0.51.
Leverage ratio approximately 1.04x EBITDA. Continued focus on gradual debt reduction through FY2026. $64.8m banked in July 2025 shows strong cash generation profile.

items.target: $0.30 per share paid during 2025, plus $0.25/share declared for April 2026
items.vs_prior: raised significantly from $0.15/share total FY2024 dividends
items.notes: 2025 payments: $0.10 (January), $0.05 (April), $0.15 (October). April 2026 declared $0.25/share. All fully imputed, DRP applies at 2% discount to VWAP. Total FY2025 capital returns of $0.55/share to shareholders.

Management stated 'too early to reliably indicate 2026'. However, noted 2025 winter chill in most regions was better than same point in 2024, lifting probability of a good 2026 season. Reemoon automation installations at Kerikeri and Huka Pak are proceeding for the 2026 harvest. Company 'enters 2026 in great shape'.

guidance.management_commentary: CEO Michael Franks noted that Seeka has 'rebuilt following the disruptions of Covid-19 followed by poor growing seasons' and described FY2025 as delivering record results. The company's near-term priorities include the 2026 automation investments (Reemoon technology at Kerikeri and Huka Pak), evaluation of a 'lights-out' automated coolstore, continued debt reduction, and building volume from new orchard developments in Raukokore and Australia. Management is deliberately cautious on FY2026 crop outlook given it is early in the growing season, though early winter chill indicators are described as positive.

bull_case: Record earnings momentum with structural underpinning: FY2025 EBITDA of $96m and NPBT of $48m are consecutive records (after the $29.7m record in FY2024). This is not solely weather-driven - automation delivered 19% cost-per-tray reduction in FY2024, labour supply has normalised, and the debt burden is falling rapidly. Net debt down 42% from peak ($172m to $100m) over two years, materially reducing interest drag.

Powerful industry tailwinds with Seeka's capacity already in place: Zespri's five-year plan targets 10% industry volume growth to 236m trays by 2030, led by SunGold expansion. Seeka has >50m tray post-harvest capacity in place without requiring major capital expenditure. As industry volumes grow, Seeka captures proportional revenue growth at high incremental margins given the largely fixed packhouse cost base.

Automation investment cycle creating durable cost advantage: Reemoon technology at Kerikeri and Huka Pak for the 2026 season represents the most advanced packing lines in Seeka's network. This automation reduces per-tray costs and reduces dependence on the RSE labour programme which faces ongoing policy risk. A potential 'lights-out' automated coolstore could be transformative for returns on coolstore assets.

Long-term orchard development pipeline building captive volume: New orchard developments (Raukokore co-investment ~70 ha, plus Australian orchards) will enter full production progressively through 2026-2030. These long-term leased orchards provide Seeka with captive fruit supply that reduces post-harvest revenue volatility versus competing for independent grower supply.

Dividend resumption signals sustainable profitability: After no dividends in 2023-2024, Seeka paid $0.30/share during 2025 and declared $0.25/share for April 2026 - a total distribution of $0.55/share in approximately 12 months. At a ~$4.60 share price, this represents a trailing yield over 10%. The board's willingness to declare these dividends reflects confidence in the underlying earnings quality and cash generation.
bear_case: Extreme earnings sensitivity to growing conditions: Seeka's FY2023 pre-tax loss of $21m on $301m revenue demonstrates how quickly profitability collapses in a poor season. A cyclone, drought, or widespread frost event affecting the Bay of Plenty (85% of supply) would repeat this outcome. Climate change is increasing the frequency and severity of such events over the long term, with research suggesting the Te Puke region faces structural growing challenges by mid-century.

Fundamental Zespri concentration and single-desk risk: Approximately 60% of Seeka's revenue flows through the Zespri system. Seeka cannot independently market kiwifruit to international markets and has limited pricing power with Zespri on post-harvest service fees. Any regulatory change to the single-desk structure, changes to Zespri's pool distributions, or deterioration in Zespri's global market performance would directly harm Seeka with no alternative outlets.

Valuation at earnings peak: The stock may be pricing in normalised continuation of record profits. The historical earnings range is extremely wide - from losses to $48m NPBT in a three-year span. Investors pricing the business on peak cycle multiples risk significant disappointment if a single poor season returns EBITDA to $30-40m (implying minimal or negative free cash flow after debt service). The business has no earnings floor.

Northern Hemisphere SunGold competition emerging: Zespri's global licensing programme has expanded SunGold production across Italy, France and other Northern Hemisphere growers. While currently complementary to NZ supply (different seasons), increasing licensed Northern Hemisphere volumes will eventually put pressure on the price premium earned for NZ-grown SunGold as total global supply rises. Zespri CEO forecasts per-tray returns moderating over the medium term as volumes grow faster than demand.

Australian expansion capital at risk: Seeka has committed $17.2m to Australian orchard developments on top of existing Australian asset investment ($70m segment assets at June 2025). Australia has historically been marginally profitable at best. The business faces Psa management challenges, lacks Seeka's NZ scale and packhouse network, and is expanding into new varieties and markets. A poor Australian growing season or market development setback would impair the value of this investment.
